name: Time-away Construction

dimensions.form: Verb head with an activity construal followed by a construction-licensed time-period direct object and the one-word PP away
dimensions.meaning: The subject uses up a bounded interval by engaging continuously or repeatedly in the verbal activity
dimensions.function: Construes a time interval as wholly occupied by an activity, often with a defeasible heedless, pleasurable, or time-wasting implication
dimensions.distribution: VP-internal; canonical Head–Od–away order, with Head–away–Od available especially for a heavy time NP

1.definition: An agentively engaged subject uses up the time interval denoted by the direct object in carrying out the verbal activity
1.details: The time NP is a genuine Od licensed by the construction, not a temporal adjunct: it passivizes, enters the tough construction, and cannot be stranded by VP ellipsis. Away is fixed and is syntactically a particle; in CGEL category terms it is an intransitive preposition heading a one-word PP complement, since particle is not a lexical category. The VP receives an activity construal: a lexical activity is normally atelic, while a repeatable bounded event such as sneeze is coerced to iteration. The heedless, pleasurable, or time-wasting implication is defeasible (Jackendoff 1997: 534–43; CGEL pp. 280–84).

examples.note: Repeatable bounded event coerced to repeated sneezing

examples.form: The evening had been nearly slept away.
examples.note: Passive evidence that the time NP is Od rather than adjunct

constraints.description: The time NP occupies Od position and excludes a lexical direct object: Fred drank the night away, not *Fred drank scotch the night away; obligatorily transitive verb uses are excluded.
Canonical order is Head–Od–away. Away may precede a sufficiently heavy NP, but modified away must follow the NP.
The NP must denote a time period; resource and activity-denoting NPs are excluded, though journey-context distance NPs can metonymically measure elapsed time.
The external subject is construed as agentively engaged and the VP denotes an activity rather than a state; the lexical verb may instead denote a repeatable bounded event.
The base activity is atelic, or a repeatable bounded event receives an iterative reading; nonrepeatable achievements are excluded.
The construction construes the interval as bounded or used up; the heedless-pleasure or should-have-done-something-else implication is conventional but defeasible.

projection.target: Recognizing Head–Od[time]–away predicts that the time NP behaves as a direct object despite lacking verb-level licensing, that away is a one-word intransitive-preposition PP in particle syntax, and that the VP denotes a bounded interval occupied by an agentive activity or iterated event
projection.evidence: Passivization, tough-construction, VP-ellipsis, particle placement, and lexical-object exclusion converge on direct-object status; independent activity, agentivity, and time-use diagnostics establish the semantic profile (Jackendoff 1997: 535–41)

grounds.note: Independent object, particle-placement, aspectual, and semantic diagnostics
The recurrent diagnostic cluster supports the stable constructional profile

diagnostics: cannot be stranded by VP ellipsis

known_boundary_items: Ordinary aspectual Head + away (work away) is atelic and has no time object; it is not the time-away construction.
The construction is distinct from the resultative and way constructions.
Distance-as-time readings are contextual extensions; activity-nominal objects are excluded.

relatedConstructions.notes: Time-away fixes away as the particle and restricts the direct object to a time-period NP
The construction-licensed time direct object is realized by an NP
Away heads the one-word PP in particle function

grounds.note: Time-object licensing, activity construal, ordering, and constructional semantics
Away is an intransitive preposition heading a one-word PP in particle use

curious.title: Sleeping the afternoon away
curious.summary: A verb, a stretch of time and the word away together say that someone spent the whole stretch on an activity.
curious.body: In Bill slept the afternoon away, the afternoon is a stretch of time that Bill fills up with sleeping. The pattern says the interval was used up by the activity, and it can suggest that the time was spent heedlessly or pleasurably, or wasted. That hint can be cancelled. The time phrase behaves like an object of the verb. It can become the subject of a passive, as in the evening had been nearly slept away. The pattern also works with a verb for a repeatable event, as in Saul sneezed the afternoon away, which means sneezing again and again. This dictionary marks the analysis as provisional.
curious.try: Think of an activity you could do for a long time, like reading or chatting. Can you say it with a stretch of time and away?

teacher.summary: Teaches how a verb, a time period and away together describe an activity that uses up an interval.
teacher.explain: The pattern is a verb with an activity construal, a time-period NP and the word away: the subject uses up the interval by engaging in the activity. The time NP is a genuine direct object licensed by the construction, not an adjunct: it passivizes and cannot be stranded by VP ellipsis. The verb gets an activity construal, so a lexical activity is atelic and a repeatable bounded event such as sneeze is read as iterated. A lexical object is excluded, as in Fred drank the night away. The heedless, pleasurable or time-wasting implication is defeasible. This dictionary marks the analysis as provisional, though its confidence is marked high.
teacher.terms: Away is traditionally called a particle or adverb. In CGEL terms it is an intransitive preposition heading a one-word PP. Od is the direct object.

contrasts.note: The time NP is the object.

contrasts.text: Fred drank scotch the night away.
contrasts.note: A lexical direct object is excluded.

contrasts.text: The evening had been nearly slept away.
contrasts.note: Passive evidence that the time NP is an object, not an adjunct.

watch_for: A learner might read the time phrase as an adjunct, when it is an object that can become the subject of a passive.
A learner might treat away as meaning leaving, when here it marks the interval as used up.
A learner might think the sentence must mean the time was wasted, when that implication can be cancelled.
teacher.activity: Give students verbs such as sleep, chat, read and sneeze. They write sentences with a time phrase and away, then decide whether the activity could fill the whole interval.

child.hook: Can you read the whole afternoon away?
child.explain: You can say you spent a whole stretch of time doing one thing. You name the time and add away. Bill slept the afternoon away means he slept for all of it.
child.play: Think of something you could do for a long time. Say it with a time like the whole morning, then away. Who can make the funniest one?
